articles.title: From Managed Security to Cyber Resilience: What We Believe the IDC MarketScape 2026 Asia/Pacific MSS Assessment Means for Security Leaders

articles.full_text:
Security leaders across Asia/Pacific are being asked to do more than watch alerts. Boards and regulators want proof that the organization can withstand an attack, contain it fast and recover with minimal disruption. That shift, from managed security to cyber resilience, is reshaping what organizations need from a security partner.

It's also the backdrop for the newly published IDC MarketScape: Asia/Pacific (Excluding Japan and China) Managed Security Services 2026 Vendor Assessment, in which LevelBlue is named a Major Player. Here's what the research tells us about the market, and why we think it matters for your security strategy.

The market: hybrid, regulated and short on talent

IDC's research paints a clear picture of how organizations across the region run security today. According to IDC's 2025 Asia/Pacific Security Survey, cited in the report:

69.9% of organizations in Asia/Pacific (excluding Japan and China) describe their security operating model as a hybrid of internal teams and external partners. Only 11.3% are fully in-house.

MSS/MDR is the second most frequently cited top-three security spending priority, at 33.3%.

When deciding whether to build, partner or outsource, buyers rank the availability of skilled talent (64.1%) and alignment with regulatory or compliance requirements (61.2%) as the two most important factors.

In other words, most organizations aren't choosing between doing it themselves and handing everything off. They want a partner that extends their team, fills skills gaps, and helps them meet a growing list of local regulatory obligations.

Accelerate your resilience to cyber threats with LevelBlue MSS.

Learn More

What IDC MarketScape said about LevelBlue

IDC MarketScape evaluated 23 providers on their current capabilities and future strategy. The report noted, “Managed security specialists (i.e., LevelBlue, Orange Cyberdefense, SISA Information Security [SISA], and Inspira Enterprise) start from threat intelligence, incident response, and detection engineering, with proprietary platforms and deep security tradecraft, although their portfolio breadth beyond managed detection and response (MDR) and regional scale vary.”

According to the report, “Clients value LevelBlue for its tailored delivery at scale, Microsoft expertise, and support for existing multivendor environments.” The IDC MarketScape also noted that “Sovereign delivery remains a key regional strength of LevelBlue.”

Four things that matter for cyber resilience

We see four themes in IDC MarketScape's assessment that we believe line up with what our clients are asking for.

Resilience across the full lifecycle. Cyber resilience means being able to prevent, detect, respond to, and recover from threats. LevelBlue brings together MXDR, co-managed SOC, exposure management, cloud and network security, identity protection, and incident readiness and response, so customers can manage cyber risk end to end rather than stitching together point services.

Intelligence that focuses effort where it counts. The IDC MarketScape notes that “Threat intelligence and exploitability-based exposure prioritization are additional strengths.” Our SpiderLabs team of more than 1,000 security professionals turns frontline incident response and research into detections and guidance that help customers act on the threats most likely to affect their business.

Sovereign-by-design delivery. In many markets, data residency and local control are no longer nice-to-haves. The IDC MarketScape describes “Its vertical fit is weighted toward regulated industries, led by BFSI, followed by critical infrastructure, government, and technology, with a substantial share of the base in regulated verticals overall. This makes LevelBlue a natural short list in which Security of Critical Infrastructure (SOCI) Act, Essential Eight, Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) Technology Risk Management (TRM), or data residency obligations are in play and ©2026 IDC #AP54132726e 14 sovereignty has become a procurement gate rather than a preference, supported by a live Australian platform instance, an Australia- and U.S.-only analyst option, and a comanaged model keeping data in the client's own tenant.” Our “Five Eyes” delivery model and the local SOC in Sydney, live since August 2026, are built for exactly those requirements.

Simplification without lock-in. Most organizations have already invested heavily in security tools. LevelBlue's vendor-agnostic approach, anchored on the Indigo Security Operations Platform, helps customers consolidate operations and get more from what they already own. The report noted, “Flexible retainers allow unused DFIR hours to support other initiatives, whereas the Response Authorization Protocol enables pre-authorized containment by asset without removing client control. Sovereign delivery remains a key regional strength of LevelBlue.” Choosing a partner, not a tool operator

The right partner for your organization depends on your size, your industry, the countries you operate in and the regulations you answer to.

If you're looking for measurable risk reduction, simpler operations and a security partner that adapts to your environment rather than the other way around, we'd welcome the conversation.

Download a complimentary excerpt of the IDC MarketScape report.

articles.title: The MSSP Handoff Problem: Where Detection Ends and Response Gets Complicated
articles.context: Managed Security Services can give security teams greater visibility and access to specialized expertise, but finding a threat is only one part of incident response
articles.full_text:
Managed Security Services can give security teams greater visibility and access to specialized expertise, but finding a threat is only one part of incident response. Once an alert becomes an incident, the operating model between an internal security team and its managed security service provider (MSSP) becomes critical.

During an active incident, several actions may need to happen quickly: validate the threat, determine its scope, isolate an endpoint, disable an account, block malicious traffic, preserve evidence, engage IT teams, and escalate to business leadership. Each action can cross organizational boundaries and require a different level of authority.

That creates an operational seam. The MSSP may have the evidence and expertise to recommend an action, while the internal team has the business context, system access, and authority to approve or execute it. Organizations that define how that seam works before an incident can move from investigation to response with fewer delays and less ambiguity. Many MSSP relationships define what the provider monitors but not who is allowed to act. That gap rarely surfaces in a service review; it surfaces during an incident, often after hours, when a containment decision is waiting on an approver nobody can reach.

As Forrester notes in their recent report, Best Practices For MDR To-IR Handoffs, "During an incident, what organizations often miss are the processes they assume are a given and will happen as a matter of course, like handoffs between providers." The challenge is the transition from threat detection to coordinated action across multiple teams and stakeholders.

Where the MSSP handoff gets complicated and an incident is declared

Consider a compromised employee account. An MSSP might identify suspicious authentication activity, correlate it with other telemetry, investigate the behavior, and determine that the account is likely compromised. The logical containment step may be to disable the account or revoke active sessions.

Taking that action introduces considerations beyond threat detection. The account could belong to an executive, administrator, service owner, or employee supporting a time-sensitive business process. The response may require coordination with identity teams, the user’s manager, IT operations, or other stakeholders.

The same challenge applies to isolating endpoints, blocking network traffic, taking servers offline, or restricting access to critical applications. Technical urgency and business impact have to be considered together.

Here is how that can play out in practice. It is 2:00 a.m. on a Saturday. The MSSP confirms the compromise and recommends revoking the user’s sessions, but the agreed process requires customer approval before acting on executive accounts. The primary contact does not answer. The backup contact changed roles months ago. By the time someone with authority approves the action, the attacker has had hours to register a new MFA device and create mail-forwarding rules. Each team did its job; the gap was in the operating model between them.

This is where the relationship between internal teams and MSSPs needs to be operationally specific. Service scope should translate into a shared understanding of what the provider investigates, what it can act on independently, which actions require customer authorization, and how responsibility changes as an incident becomes more severe.

Accelerate your resilience to cyber threats with LevelBlue MSS.

Learn More

Those expectations should also extend beyond normal business hours. A response model that depends on reaching one specific internal contact can create a bottleneck during nights, weekends, or holidays. Organizations need primary and backup contacts, defined escalation thresholds, and predetermined rules for situations where an authorized decision-maker cannot immediately be reached.

The handoff also changes character at a specific point: when someone declares an incident. Before that point, the MSSP is triaging and escalating alerts. After it, the organization’s incident response plan takes over, an incident commander assumes coordination, often under external counsel, and obligations such as evidence preservation, regulatory notification timelines, and cyber insurance reporting may begin. The escalation framework should name who can make that declaration, what criteria trigger it, and how the MSSP’s role shifts once it is made.

Forrester warns that "Misaligned handoff protocols between MDR and IR providers lead to conflicting direction, inconsistent situational context, and slowed decision-making during the most time-critical phases of an incident."

For high-severity scenarios such as ransomware or confirmed data exfiltration, the response often extends well beyond the internal team and the MSSP. Breach counsel may be engaged early, the cyber insurer may require an approved incident response firm , and dedicated forensics teams may take over scoping. In many cases, these stakeholders are brought together only after a major incident occurs, making it critical to define expectations in advance around roles, decision authority, evidence sharing, communications, and reporting requirements.

Define four types of ownership

A practical escalation framework can start by assigning four types of ownership: investigation, containment, communication, and decision-making.

Investigation ownership establishes how far the MSSP should take an investigation before escalating it. Internal teams should know what information will arrive with that escalation, including affected assets and identities, indicators of compromise, investigation steps, severity, supporting evidence, and recommended actions. A consistent evidence package allows the internal team to build on the provider’s work rather than retracing it. Investigation should also account for a common transition during major incidents: the handoff from the MSSP’s security operations center (SOC) team to a digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) team. With many providers, that escalation involves a third party, which can introduce delays while contracts are activated, accounts are provisioned, access to data is established, and new investigators are brought up to speed. Organizations should define in advance how that transition occurs, what information is transferred, and who maintains continuity throughout the investigation. Providers with integrated MSSP and DFIR capabilities can help reduce additional friction during this phase of the response.

Containment ownership defines who has authority to disrupt potentially malicious activity. Organizations should document who can isolate an endpoint, disable an account, block infrastructure, quarantine messages, restrict network access, or take a system offline. Some organizations may authorize their managed security service provider to perform predetermined actions under defined conditions, while others may require internal approval. The important consideration is that both parties understand the boundaries and the process for exceptions. Containment ownership should also account for evidence: reimaging a system or deleting malicious artifacts too quickly can destroy the forensic data needed to understand scope. Ownership should extend beyond initial containment into recovery activities, including heightened monitoring, validation that the threat actor has been removed, and decisions about when systems can safely return to production. Unclear communication between internal teams, the MSSP, and third-party responders during this phase can create new risks, such as restoring access too soon or unnecessarily extending operational disruptions.

Communication ownership connects the security response with the rest of the organization. IT operations may need to rebuild devices. Identity teams may need to revoke credentials. Application owners can provide context about affected systems. Legal, privacy, communications, and executive teams may need to participate as severity increases. The escalation framework should identify who engages these stakeholders, through which channels, and at what point in the response.

Decision ownership becomes increasingly important as potential business impact grows. The team performing technical analysis may recommend containment, while an incident commander or business leader holds authority to approve an action with significant operational consequences. Severity levels should therefore map to specific decision-makers, including alternates when the primary owner is unavailable.

Clearly separating these responsibilities helps an organization use managed cybersecurity services as part of a broader incident response model rather than treating the provider relationship as an isolated security function.

Build escalation paths around scenarios

A useful escalation plan needs more than a contact list. It should map realistic incident scenarios to specific responsibilities, authority, communication channels, and expected response times.

For common scenarios such as compromised credentials, ransomware, cloud account abuse, suspected data exfiltration, or malware on a critical server, teams can document:

Trigger: What evidence or severity initiates escalation?

Investigator: Who validates the activity and determines scope?

Decision-maker: Who has authority to approve containment?

Executor: Who performs the technical action?

Communicator: Who coordinates with IT and other stakeholders?

Fallback: Who assumes responsibility if the primary contact is unavailable?

Time threshold: How long should the process wait for a decision before moving to the next escalation point?

The framework should be documented in incident response plans and playbooks, then be tested through tabletop exercises and operational reviews. Exercises can reveal outdated contact information, unclear approval authority, after-hours communication gaps, or technical actions that cannot be executed as expected. Real incidents can provide another feedback loop. If responders repeatedly lose time identifying an application owner or securing approval for containment, that friction points to a process that needs refinement.

This approach also acknowledges that the handoff is rarely a single moment. Investigation, containment, recovery, and communication may pass between an MSSP, the internal security team, IT, and business stakeholders several times over the course of one incident.

The larger challenge is not simply transferring responsibility from an MSSP to a customer. It is transitioning from a technical finding to the business decisions that follow. An MSSP may identify a compromised account, active ransomware, or suspected data exfiltration, but decisions about containment, recovery, communications, legal obligations, and operational risk ultimately belong to the organization.

Effective managed cybersecurity services depend on those transitions being deliberate. By defining who investigates, who contains, who communicates, and who decides, organizations can connect external security expertise with internal authority and business context.

An incident should put an escalation plan into action, rather than expose where one was missing.

LevelBlue helps organizations define these responsibilities before an incident tests them, through incident response planning and tabletop exercises that pressure-test escalation paths with both internal teams and their security providers.

Source: Jess Burn, Jeff Pollard, Joseph Blankenship, Liam Holloway, and Michael Belden, "Best Practices for MDR-to-IR Handoffs," Forrester Research, March 13, 2026.

Contributions by Kenneth Ng, Director of Operational Intelligence at LevelBlue.

articles.title: LevelBlue and rrelentless: Bringing Proactive Cyber Resilience to Cyber Insurance Policyholders
articles.context: Why cyber insurance needs security expertise built in Threats evolve constantly, and a policy that only pays out after a breach leaves organizations to manage that risk on their...
articles.full_text:
Cyber insurance has traditionally done its most important work after something goes wrong. We think it can do much more before an incident ever happens.

That's why LevelBlue is partnering with rrelentless, a UK-based specialist Managing General Agent (MGA), to give its cyber insurance policyholders access to LevelBlue's cybersecurity expertise as part of their policy. Every rrelentless cyber policyholder can now tap into LevelBlue Security Colony, gaining practical tools and expert guidance to understand their exposure, prioritize improvements and build resilience day to day.

Why cyber insurance needs security expertise built in

Threats evolve constantly, and a policy that only pays out after a breach leaves organizations to manage that risk on their own the rest of the time. Many small and mid-sized businesses don't have the in-house security staff to know where their weaknesses are, let alone fix them.

rrelentless shares our view that insurance should play an active role in reducing risk, not just transferring it. By embedding LevelBlue's services directly into its cyber policies, rrelentless gives policyholders a clear path to find vulnerabilities, assess their readiness and act on them before a claim is ever needed. That's good for the businesses, and good for the long-term health of the cyber insurance market.

What rrelentless policyholders get with LevelBlue

Through LevelBlue Security Colony, rrelentless cyber policyholders can access a suite of proactive services, exclusive to rrelentless customers and included with every cyber policy:

Vulnerability scanning to identify technical weaknesses across their environment

Cyber maturity assessments to benchmark their security posture and prioritize what to improve first

Ransomware readiness assessments to understand how prepared they are for one of today's most damaging threats

Vendor risk assessments to evaluate the security of the third parties they rely on

Unlock exclusive rrelentless access to Security Colony.

Learn More

Breach monitoring to spot potential exposure of their data early

Ask the Expert forum access, connecting them directly with LevelBlue security specialists

Together, these services turn a cyber policy into an ongoing resource for improving security, not just a safety net.

Resilience starts with understanding risk

"Cyber resilience begins with understanding where risk exists and having clear, practical guidance to address it," said Grant Duncan, SVP at LevelBlue. "Through this partnership, rrelentless policyholders will gain access to LevelBlue's Security Colony, connecting them with expert insights and practical resources to better understand their cyber exposure, prioritize areas for improvement, and strengthen their internal security capabilities."

"By combining LevelBlue's cybersecurity expertise with rrelentless' proactive approach to risk management, we can help more policyholders take meaningful action before an incident occurs, reduce risk, and build lasting resilience."

Gary Gallen, Chief Executive of rrelentless and its parent, the rradar group of companies, sees the partnership the same way: "Cyber risk does not stand still, so neither can cyber insurance. Partnering with global cyber specialists LevelBlue and Pistachio and leveraging the power of their expertise will bring significant value to our customers."

Part of a 360-degree view of cyber risk

LevelBlue's technical services sit alongside two other layers of support in the rrelentless cyber proposition. Legal firm rradar provides specialist cyber legal, regulatory and risk management guidance. Security awareness training provider Pistachio, which joins as a partner at the same time, offers personalized training, simulated phishing campaigns and behavioral insights to strengthen the human side of security.

The result is legal, technical and people-focused support before, during and after a cyber incident, with LevelBlue providing the technical insight that helps policyholders see and close their gaps.

Bringing LevelBlue expertise to more organizations

As the world's largest and most analyst-recognized pure-play managed security service provider, LevelBlue supports thousands of organizations across 96 countries with managed security services, threat intelligence and risk consulting. Partnerships like this one with rrelentless let us extend that expertise to businesses that might otherwise never have access to it, through a channel they already trust.

We're proud to help rrelentless policyholders take meaningful action before an incident occurs. To learn more about LevelBlue Security Colony and our partnerships with insurers and MGAs, visit LevelBlue.com. Businesses interested in rrelentless cyber insurance should speak to their insurance broker, and brokers can contact brokerenquiry@rrelentless.com.

articles.title: Is Your Refrigerator Running? Yes, It’s Running an Outdated OS: What the Supermarket Refrigeration Attacks Reveal About Embedded Security
articles.context: The saddest part here: A firmware fix was available at the time of attack
articles.full_text:
Overnight on November 2, freezers in supermarkets across Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg and Ireland climbed to around 50°C, and stores awoke to spoiled stock. This is the second wave within a month, after a similar attack on hundreds of French stores in October. No one has publicly claimed either attack, and the attack vector hasn't been confirmed.

Regardless of who is responsible, the targets are what should worry us. These were refrigeration controllers: small, purpose-built devices that most of their asset owners likely didn’t think of as computers at all.

Invisible by design

The first problem is that nobody is looking for, or often even aware these devices are network connected. These devices often become effectively invisible once the integrator puts them in place. They perform their function reliably, and quietly. Unless something breaks, nobody thinks about them as computers that need ongoing security maintenance.

A refrigeration controller is installed by a contractor, commissioned, and then left to run. It rarely appears in an IT asset inventory, it often sits outside the security team's remit, and even worse, it may be reachable remotely so the maintenance provider can service it. That combination: connected, unmonitored, and effectively unowned, is an attacker’s dream target.

A patching problem with no easy fix

That invisibility creates a serious patching problem. Many embedded and industrial devices remain exposed not only to recently disclosed vulnerabilities, but also to flaws that were remediated decades ago, along with product-specific firmware weaknesses that may never be publicly documented.

The gaps come in several forms:

No fix exists. The manufacturer is unaware of the issue, has ended support for the product, or has no incentive to address it.

A fix exists but never reaches the field. The operator may not realize the device is vulnerable, may not know an upstream update is available, or may no longer have a clear owner responsible for maintaining it.

The fix is difficult to apply. There usually is no equivalent of Windows Update or Linux's `yum`/`apt` that can centrally track and deliver these updates. Updates may require a technician, a vendor-specific utility, physical access, or downtime that operators are reluctant to schedule.

Advance your IoT security with LevelBlue.

Learn More

The French attack shows how this plays out. Intermarché's owner said its systems were managed by Danfoss (an external engineering/product firm), and Reuters reported some of the November targets used the same technology. In August, Claroty's Team82 disclosed flaws in Danfoss refrigeration controllers, including a hidden credential that could grant admin access, and found thousands of the controllers reachable from the internet. The saddest part here: A firmware fix was available at the time of attack. Whether those flaws were used hasn't been established, but a fix that has been released is not the same as a fleet that has been patched.

Built for a different era, kept for decades

A lot of this equipment was also designed in an era, or for an environment, where security was not only not a primary focus, but often wasn't even considered. As a result, you still encounter weaknesses that the broader software industry has treated as solved problems for years: weak authentication, exposed services, hard-coded credentials, insecure update mechanisms, and other basic issues.

Those weaknesses persist because the hardware does. These devices can remain operational long after the vendor has ended support or stopped producing security updates. From an operational perspective, replacing a device that still does its job can be difficult to justify, even though it may be extremely vulnerable.

And even when manufacturers consider software security, hardware security often remains unaccounted for. Maintenance and debugging interfaces intended for technicians can sometimes provide surprisingly direct access to a device if someone can reach it physically. Features that are useful during manufacturing or servicing can become security liabilities when equipment remains deployed unattended, and a rooftop condenser or back-room controller cabinet is about as unattended as equipment gets.

This isn't a supermarket problem

It would be easy to file these attacks under retail and move on, but that misses the point. The broader issue is not at all specific to supermarkets or refrigeration. These kinds of niche embedded and IoT systems are deployed across retail, manufacturing, building automation, healthcare, critical infrastructure, solar, agriculture, and many other industries.

They are everywhere, but because they are purpose-built and usually quietly doing their jobs, they are often overlooked until an incident makes them visible. This month, that incident was spoiled food. In another sector, the same class of weakness could mean a stalled production line, a building with no climate control, disrupted energy assets causing blackouts, or tainted water at a utility.

What to do now

Organizations running embedded, IoT, and OT equipment, in stores or anywhere else can reduce exposure with a few practical steps:

Understand what you have. Inventory every connected device, including those installed and managed by third-party integrators, record the firmware version of each, and note the update mechanism/method.

Assign an owner and write processes. Every device needs a named person or team responsible for its security, not just its uptime, and they need to be aware of how to properly patch the device.

Take it off the internet. Devices should not be directly reachable from the public internet. Put remote vendor access behind a VPN or secure gateway with MFA and logging.

Patch, and plan for what you can't patch. Check vendor advisories, schedule firmware updates, and segment or monitor devices that are out of support until they can be replaced.

Change the defaults. Remove shared and default credentials and ask vendors directly about hidden or maintenance accounts.

Protect physical access. Secure cabinets and service ports on unattended equipment.

Alert on the physical outcome. Independent temperature or process alarms can catch tampering that the compromised controller itself would hide. Establish a baseline and expected value ranges, find a way to track them, and alert on them if they deviate.

Test it. Product (hardware/firmware) and OT- focused penetration testing finds the forgotten device before an attacker does.

The freezers in Sweden, Belgium, and France were doing exactly what they were built to do, until someone else told them otherwise. The lesson is simple: if it runs code, it can be compromised. And if your business depends on it, you can't afford to pretend it's just an appliance.

articles.title: LevelBlue Named Editor's Choice for Managed Detection and Response in the 2026 Top InfoSec Innovators Awards
articles.context: LevelBlue has been named Editor's Choice for Managed Detection and Response (MDR) in Cyber Defense Magazine's Top InfoSec Innovators awards for 2026
articles.full_text:
LevelBlue has been named Editor's Choice for Managed Detection and Response (MDR) in Cyber Defense Magazine's Top InfoSec Innovators awards for 2026. The award was announced on October 20, 2026, during CyberDefenseCon 2026 in Orlando, Florida.

It's a recognition we're especially proud of. MDR sits at the heart of what LevelBlue does every day: helping organizations detect threats faster, respond with confidence, and stay one step ahead of attackers.

About the Top InfoSec Innovators Awards

Now in its 14th year, Cyber Defense Magazine's awards program honors the cybersecurity companies doing the most to get ahead of tomorrow's threats. Winners are chosen by a panel of industry veterans and investors, including Ron Gula of Gula Tech Adventures, Gary Miliefsky of Cyber Defense Media Group, Katie Gray of In-Q-Tel, and Robert R. Ackerman Jr. of DataTribe.

The Top InfoSec Innovators are announced each fall at CyberDefenseCon, an invitation-only gathering of top global CISOs. This year's list recognizes 147 companies, and you can see the full list of 2026 winners on the Cyber Defense Awards site.

"LevelBlue embodies three major features we judges look for with the potential to become winners: understanding tomorrow's threats, today, providing a cost-effective solution and innovating in unexpected ways that can help mitigate cyber risk and get one step ahead of the next breach," said Gary S. Miliefsky, Publisher of Cyber Defense Magazine.

Eliminate threats quickly and precisely with proven MDR.

Learn More

What sets LevelBlue MDR apart

As the world's largest pure-play managed security service provider, LevelBlue brings together intelligence-led security, AI-powered managed services, and deep cyber expertise to stop threats faster. Our MDR offering draws on the combined strengths of Trustwave, Cybereason and Alert Logic, each a long-standing name in detection and response, now united under one roof.

That combination gives customers:

Round-the-clock detection and response from experienced security operations teams

Threat intelligence that turns visibility across thousands of organizations into faster, better-informed action

Incident response readiness, so organizations know exactly what to do when an alert becomes an incident

Flexibility to protect cloud, hybrid and on-premises environments, including regulated and high-risk industries

A track record of recognition

This is the third year in a row that LevelBlue has been named a Top InfoSec Innovator, and the latest in a long run of Cyber Defense Magazine honors for the teams that now make up LevelBlue.

In 2025, LevelBlue was named Market Leader for Managed Security Service Provider (MSSP), Most Innovative for Threat Exposure Management and Publisher's Choice for Unified Threat Management. In 2024, we won Best Solution for MDR Provider, plus Publisher's Choice honors in Security Consulting and Threat Intelligence, and in 2023, AT&T Cybersecurity (now LevelBlue) was named Most Innovative in Threat Intelligence. Trustwave, now part of LevelBlue, built its own MDR track record in Cyber Defense Magazine's sister program, the Global InfoSec Awards, announced each spring at RSAC. It was named Market Leader for Global Managed Threat Detection and Response in 2021, Best Solution for both Cloud MDR Provider and Global MDR Service Provider in 2022, and Editor's Choice for MDR Service Providers in 2023. Across the two programs, LevelBlue and Trustwave have now been recognized for MDR in five of the last six years.

Thank you to our teams and customers

This recognition belongs to our security operations teams, who work around the clock to detect and stop threats, and to the customers who trust us to protect what matters most.

We're grateful to Cyber Defense Magazine and its judges for this recognition. To learn how LevelBlue MDR can help your organization detect and respond to threats faster, explore our MDR services or talk to an expert.

articles.title: Keep Cyber Threats Out of Play: Five Cybersecurity Tips for Golf Facilities
articles.context: Helping PGA of America Golf Professionals address those questions is part of the Association’s partnership with LevelBlue, the Official Cybersecurity Advisor of the PGA of...
articles.full_text:
Originally published by the PGA of America.

Operating a golf facility means keeping track of a lot more than what’s happening on the course. Tee times, lesson schedules, payroll and vendor payments all depend on technology working as it should. Keeping those systems secure is easy to put off when everything is running smoothly, but it’s worth making time before a problem interrupts the day.

October’s Cybersecurity Awareness Month is a good opportunity to sit down with your team or technology provider and ask a few questions: Who has access to your accounts? How do employees flag a suspicious email? What’s the plan if your booking system goes down?

Helping PGA of America Golf Professionals address those questions is part of the Association’s partnership with LevelBlue, the Official Cybersecurity Advisor of the PGA of America, PGA Championship and KPMG Women’s PGA Championship through 2028. LevelBlue provides services to help protect the Association’s technology and flagship events, while also bringing cybersecurity education to the broader golf community.

Discover why LevelBlue is the Official Cybersecurity Advisor of the PGA of America.

Learn More

“Our PGA of America Members have a lot on their plates, and cybersecurity may not be their area of expertise,” said Kevin Scott, Chief Technology Officer, PGA of America. “Working with LevelBlue helps us bring them practical information they can use when talking with their staff and technology providers.”

Five places to start

Check your logins. Use a different password for each account and a password manager to keep track of them. Turn on multifactor authentication, which requires another verification step when you sign in. Start with email, financial systems and accounts with administrative access.

Give staff permission to pause. An email asking for an urgent payment or new banking details should prompt a phone call to a number you already trust. Make sure employees know whom to ask when something seems off, even if the request appears to come from the boss.

Ask who handles updates. Your reservation software, shop computers and other devices need regular security updates. Confirm with your providers who installs security updates and how quickly they’re applied. Don’t assume someone else has it covered.

Remove access when people leave. When a seasonal employee finishes or a vendor relationship ends, removing their access should be part of the process. For current staff, check that each person has access only to what their job requires.

Talk through an outage. Decide how staff members would handle check-in and other essential tasks without access to your usual systems. Keep your technology provider’s contact details handy, ask about backups and recovery, and practice the plan with your team.

You don’t need to tackle everything in one meeting. Pick a starting point, assign someone to follow up and put time on the calendar to check progress. Revisit the discussion when you bring on new staff, change providers or add a system.

articles.title: Do Your Security Tools Actually Work Together? Assessing Your Zero Trust Readiness
articles.context: They purchased one tool to address an immediate threat, added another to meet a compliance requirement, and introduced others as the business adopted cloud services, supported...
articles.full_text:
LevelBlue’s free Zero Trust Readiness Review helps organizations uncover security gaps and get more value from their existing investments.

One of the first questions I ask security leaders is simple: Do you know whether all your security tools work together?

The answer is rarely a straightforward yes.

Most organizations have built their security environments over many years. They purchased one tool to address an immediate threat, added another to meet a compliance requirement, and introduced others as the business adopted cloud services, supported remote work, or completed an acquisition. Each decision may have made sense at the time, but few organizations have had the opportunity to step back and evaluate the environment as a whole.

That is why we developed LevelBlue’s free Zero Trust Readiness Review. In roughly three days, one of our Solution Architects evaluates an organization’s security posture across identity, networks, devices, applications, data, and visibility. The review is aligned with the NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture framework, and the organization receives a written report identifying potential gaps and opportunities to get more value from its existing security investments.

There is no cost, no obligation, and no predetermined platform to adopt. The organization owns the findings and decides what to do with them.

More tools do not necessarily mean better security

When I talk with security teams, I often find that the challenge is not a lack of technology. In many cases, the organization already owns many of the capabilities it needs.

The harder question is whether those capabilities are configured correctly, connected where they need to be, and supported by processes that allow the team to act on the information they produce.

For example, one tool may identify suspicious activity, while another contains the information needed to determine whether that activity is truly a threat. If the tools do not exchange information, or if the right team does not receive it quickly enough, both technologies can be working as designed while the organization still lacks the visibility needed to respond effectively.

Take the first step toward Zero Trust with the LevelBlue Readiness Review.

Learn More

We also see organizations paying for overlapping capabilities or leaving valuable features unused. That does not necessarily mean they made poor purchasing decisions. Their business, technology environment, and risk profile may simply have changed since those decisions were made.

The problem is that these inefficiencies and gaps can be difficult to recognize when every tool is evaluated individually. Security leaders need to see how the entire environment functions together.

Zero Trust is not something you can buy

Another question I frequently hear is: What product do we need to implement Zero Trust?

My answer is that Zero Trust is not a product. It is an architectural approach based on continuously evaluating access according to identity, context, risk, and the sensitivity of the resource involved.

No single platform can establish that model on its own.

An effective Zero Trust strategy depends on how identity, networks, devices, applications, data, and security visibility work together. A weakness in any one of those areas can undermine otherwise strong controls. Even sophisticated technology can fall short when policies, integrations, and operational processes do not support it.

That is why I believe a Zero Trust review should begin with the environment an organization already has, not with a predetermined list of products it is expected to purchase.

Some of the most useful questions are also the most practical:

Can you consistently verify who and what is requesting access?

Are access decisions informed by device health, user behavior, and other relevant context?

Can your security team connect related activity across the environment?

Are applications and data protected according to their sensitivity and importance to the business?

Do your existing tools share the information needed to detect and respond to threats?

Are you paying for redundant capabilities or leaving valuable features unused?

These questions help establish a realistic view of where an organization stands today. The objective is not to declare that an organization has either “achieved” or “failed” Zero Trust.

It is to identify the gaps that matter most and determine what practical improvements should come next.

The next investment may not be another tool

Security teams are being asked to reduce risk while operating under tighter budget and resource constraints. In that environment, buying another product should not always be the first response.

Sometimes the fastest way to improve security is to enable a capability the organization already owns. It may be correcting a configuration, connecting two systems that currently operate separately, or improving the process for investigating and escalating alerts. In other cases, a review may confirm that a genuine capability gap exists and that a new investment is warranted.

Both outcomes are valuable. The point is to make that decision with a clear understanding of the existing environment.

I also encourage security leaders to consider how they will communicate the findings outside the security organization. A technically accurate assessment has limited value if it cannot help the CISO explain risks, priorities, and investment needs to other executives or the board.

That is why our Zero Trust Readiness Review concludes with a written report in plain language. It provides a practical summary of where the organization stands, why the identified gaps matter, and which actions could have the greatest impact.

Start with a clear view of where you are

Zero Trust is a continuing process, not a one-time project. Technologies, business requirements, and threats will continue to change, and an organization’s security architecture must evolve with them.

But before security leaders can determine where to go next, they need an honest view of where they are today.

My advice is to begin by looking at what you already own. Understand how your tools work together, where visibility breaks down, and whether your current investments support the outcomes your organization needs. That foundation will help you focus your resources, establish defensible priorities, and make future decisions with greater confidence.

Ready to see how your security tools work together? Book your free Zero Trust Readiness Review.

The Zero Trust Readiness Review is not a compliance audit, certification, or attestation against NIST SP 800-207.
